clinicalPearls: Fixed obstruction below the aortic valve, most often from a discrete fibrous or fibromuscular ridge in the left ventricular outflow tract
It is usually acquired and progressive during childhood, and may recur after resection
The turbulent subvalvular jet can damage the aortic valve, causing progressive aortic regurgitation
It must be distinguished from valvular aortic stenosis and from hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (a dynamic obstruction)
An ejection systolic murmur is heard, and unlike valvular stenosis there is no ejection click
Surgical resection is considered for significant gradients or progressive aortic regurgitation, but recurrence is common
reference.pathophysiology: Discrete subaortic stenosis is characterised by a fibrous or fibromuscular membrane or ridge in the left ventricular outflow tract beneath the aortic valve, producing a fixed obstruction to ejection. Abnormal outflow tract geometry and shear stress are thought to stimulate proliferation of the obstructing tissue, which explains its progressive nature and tendency to recur after removal. The high-velocity subvalvular jet strikes the aortic valve leaflets, causing thickening and regurgitation over time, while the pressure-loaded left ventricle hypertrophies.
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography localising the obstruction and measuring the gradient
Assessment of aortic valve for secondary regurgitation
Evaluation of left ventricular hypertrophy and function
Exclusion of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and valvular stenosis
Serial follow-up given progression and recurrence
redFlags: Symptoms of outflow obstruction (syncope, angina, breathlessness)
reference.prognosis: Resection relieves the obstruction and can protect the aortic valve, but the lesion may recur and aortic regurgitation can persist, so long-term surveillance is required.
pitfalls: Confusing fixed subaortic stenosis with dynamic hypertrophic obstruction
Overlooking progressive aortic regurgitation from the subvalvular jet
Assuming cure after resection without follow-up for recurrence
management: Surgical resection of the obstructing fibrous or fibromuscular membrane, with septal myectomy where fibromuscular, for a significant gradient or progressive aortic regurgitation
Serial echocardiographic surveillance of the outflow gradient, aortic valve and left ventricular hypertrophy given the tendency to progress and to recur after resection
Monitor for and manage progressive aortic regurgitation caused by the high-velocity subvalvular jet damaging the valve leaflets
Endocarditis prevention through good dental and oral hygiene, with antibiotic prophylaxis where indicated
Reoperation for recurrent obstruction, which is common after initial resection
Referral to congenital or structural cardiology and cardiac surgery for timing of intervention
